text.why: Expository preaching expounds the teaching of this text. Everything you say has to come from here, not from what you would like to say.
text.b1: Read the passage several times, until you see it whole rather than in pieces.
text.b2: Tap the key words: the ones that repeat, the ones the author explains himself, and the ones that carry the action or the argument forward.
text.b3: For now you are only observing. The sermon idea comes later.

observation.why: Key words are recognised by three signs: they repeat in the text, the biblical writer explains them himself, or they matter to how the action or the argument unfolds.
observation.b1: What repeats? Repetition is the surest sign (see 2 Corinthians 1:3-11 or Luke 2:25-27).
observation.b2: What contrasts or antitheses does the author set side by side?
observation.b3: Who does what? Which verbs drive the text forward?
observation.b4: Where is the tension of the text — the problem it resolves?

context.why: A text taken out of context becomes a pretext. Context shows you what the author meant, not what we would find convenient for him to mean.
context.b1: Literary: which genre it is (narrative, poetry, epistle, prophecy, parable, proverb) and where the passage falls in the chapter and the book.
context.b2: Cultural: the world the writer, the characters and the recipients came from.
context.b3: Historical: the circumstances in which the action happens or the words are spoken.
context.b4: Geographical: sometimes the terrain or the distance between cities explains the text (Exodus 14).
context.b5: Theological: what the author, the characters and the recipients believed about God (Genesis 12:10-20).

idea.why: This is where the sermon is decided, and you get there in three steps: what the text said then, what God wants to change now, and how that is said today.
idea.b1: The exegetical idea sums up the teaching of the text for its original recipients. To be sound it must contain the subject (what is the text about?) and what is said about that subject.
idea.b2: The purpose answers a single question: what does God want to change in the hearers? It may touch their convictions, their character or their conduct.
idea.b3: The homiletical idea is the exegetical idea restated and brought up to date, in the light of the purpose.
idea.b4: The homiletical idea must be exegetically faithful, clearly worded, comprehensive, concise and relevant to the hearers.
idea.quote: "When the idea appears in the preacher’s mind as clear as a cloudless moon, then he has the message he ought to preach." (Robinson)
idea.e1: Exegetical idea: the grace of God must change people’s lives because of the high price Christ paid to redeem his people.
idea.e2: Purpose: that people would want grace for a changed life, not for free favours.
idea.e3: Homiletical idea: the grace of God is a power at work, not merely a favour.
idea.warn: This is the hardest step of the whole preparation. Do not move on until you have it clear.

structure.why: The divisions argue, explain or apply the homiletical idea. You obtain them by putting an analytical question to it: Why? How? When? On what conditions? What does it mean?
structure.b1: Word them concisely, but not vaguely.
structure.b2: Make them symmetrical: starting with the same group of words and sharing the same grammatical shape.
structure.b3: Order them progressively, so they carry the hearer towards a moment of decision.
structure.b4: Attach to each division the verse it comes from: the reference is the authority behind it.
structure.b5: Put a transition sentence between divisions, so the hearer knows you have moved on.
structure.e1: Analytical question: WHAT does that power work?
structure.e2: 1. The grace of God transforms believers’ lives (v. 11-12)
structure.e3: 2. The grace of God offers them hope (v. 13)
structure.e4: 3. The grace of God gives their life meaning (v. 14)

development.why: Each division is developed through three sections: explaining and applying are required, illustrating is optional.
development.b1: Explain the meaning of the concept as it appears in the preaching text, not across the whole of Scripture. Other verses come in only insofar as they help understand it here.
development.b2: Apply: applications connect Scripture to the hearers and decide the relevance of the sermon. Answer two questions — what do the characters of the text and the hearers have in common, and when are they in that same situation?
development.b3: Illustrate: a story that shows the stated truth in practice. Keep it tied to the division, original, believable, easy to follow and short.
development.b4: You can also develop by subdivisions, putting analytical questions to the concept of the division: how? which? why? what does it involve? what are the consequences?

final.why: The conclusion does not summarize the sermon, it closes it: restating the idea and looking at what changes if the hearer applies it.
final.b1: It has three parts: restating the homiletical idea, recapping the divisions, and the vision — what will happen if the hearers apply the idea.

transition.title: How to write it
transition.how: Number of divisions + the key word in the plural + the analytical question. It announces what you are about to say without giving away the first point yet. The key word belongs here, not in the wording of the divisions.
transition.pick: Tap a suggestion to use it as a starting point.
transition.s1: Let us look together at three REASONS why…
transition.s2: The text shows us four STEPS by which…
transition.s3: Here are two CONDITIONS that God sets…

textual.text: The text is short — a verse or two. Mark its words: the divisions will come out of them.
textual.observation: In a short text every word carries weight. Do not hunt for repetitions the text does not have: look at each word on its own and at how they hold together.
textual.context: Context counts double here: a verse pulled out of its paragraph can be made to say anything. Read the whole chapter before deciding what your verse says.
textual.idea: The idea also comes from that short text, not from the subject it suggests to you. If you have arrived at an idea the text does not support, you have moved to a thematic sermon.
textual.structure: The divisions come from the parts of the short text — clauses, key words — not from other passages. Other verses belong in Development, as support.
textual.development: This is where the other passages come in, as support for what your text already says. They explain it; they do not replace it.
textual.final: The conclusion returns to the verse you started from. The listener should leave knowing by heart the short text you preached.
textual.intro: The introduction leads toward the short verse, not toward a broader subject you could draw from it.

thematic.text: This is the base text. In a thematic sermon each division rests on a different passage: add them as references in the Development step.
thematic.observation: Observe the base text, not the subject. The subject is already in plain sight; what you have to find out is what this passage says about it, in its own words.
thematic.context: Every passage you are going to use has its own context, not just the base one. A verse that says something else in context does not go into the sermon, however well it sounds.
thematic.idea: The exegetical idea comes from the base text; the other passages support it, they do not change it. If the idea cannot be drawn from any text, it is yours and not Scripture’s.
thematic.structure: Each division has its own passage. Check every verse in its context: if it does not say there what you are saying, drop it rather than force it.
thematic.development: The danger here is the string of proof texts. Each passage gets a brief explanation in its own context; otherwise the sermon is a list of quotations with no teaching in it.
thematic.final: The conclusion gathers the subject into a single sentence. If the listener cannot say on the way out what it was about, the subject was too broad.
thematic.intro: The introduction can start from the subject, not necessarily from the base text — but the applications still have to come from the hearer’s life.

intro.why: It is written now, with the idea and structure already clear — not at the end, as the course teaches. It has two parts; the transition to the first point is a separate field, already written in Structure.
intro.b1: The opening sentence comes out of the homiletical idea or the subject, tied to the hearers’ everyday life.
intro.b2: The introductory applications bring the hearer’s need to the surface and create positive tension. Without it, the sermon is the answer to a question nobody asked.
intro.b3: Do not begin with technical detail about the book or about its recipients.
intro.b4: If you do not yet know where you are going, you can skip this step and come back after writing Development — nothing here is required.

meta.title: The Bible that does not track you. 4 languages. No ads.
meta.description: RoBible is a free web app for reading, searching and studying the Bible. No trackers, no ads, no marketing cookies. In Romanian, Spanish, English and Chinese.

hero.title: Scripture you can trust. And in your pocket.
hero.lede: 66 books. 31,102 verses. 4 languages. Smart search, version comparison, synced notes — all without ads, trackers, or subscriptions.

demo.hint: Type a reference (e.g. rom 3 5) and press Enter — we take you to the verse, highlighted in green.
demo.no_results: No results. Try another format (e.g. rom 3 5, 1co 13 4, acts 2 38).

features.title: Features built for serious study — and comfortable reading.

f1.title: Reference search, not index lookup
f1.text: Type 'rom 3 5' or '1 john 2 6' or 'genesis 1:1' and you arrive directly. Diacritics and typos are handled.

f2.title: Search the text, not just quotes
f2.text: Search words, phrases, or combinations. You can search the whole Bible, a single testament, or one book.

f3.title: Compare versions, verse by verse
f3.text: See the same passage in two translations, side by side. Useful for deep study or teaching.

f4.title: Notes and favorites in the cloud
f4.text: Write notes on verses, group them by topic, save favorites. Everything syncs across devices, free, no card.
f4.example: Your note on John 3:16 — on phone, tablet, laptop.

why.title: Because a Bible should not be a product.
why.lede: We don't want your money, your attention, or your data. We just want you to read Scripture without obstacles.

w1.title: No trackers. No ads. No marketing cookies.
w1.text: No Google Analytics, no Facebook Pixel, no sponsored content. You read, that's it.

w2.title: Works offline (PWA).
w2.text: Install the app on your phone. It downloads once, then works without internet. Perfect for travel, sermons, retreats.

w3.title: 4 languages from day one: ro, es, en, zh.
w3.text: We don't add languages for marketing. We add them because everyone deserves Scripture in their own tongue.

w4.title: Open source. No surprises.
w4.text: The code is on GitHub. If you don't like a decision, you can change it. Or find someone who will.

p1.title: Individual study
p1.text: You read, search, take notes. No distraction, no mandatory account, no ads between verses.

p2.title: Teaching and group study
p2.text: Compare translations, take notes by topic, prepare lessons without fighting the interface.

p3.title: Just curiosity
p3.text: You want to find a quote you heard on the radio. You don't need an account. You type and find.

compare.title: What we have. What we don't. No promises.
compare.lede: We don't claim to be perfect. Here is what we offer — and what we don't — against typical Bible apps.

faq.title: What you did not find elsewhere
faq.a1: Yes, completely. No ads, no subscription, no card. The project is sustained by volunteer work and optional donations.
faq.a2: Notes and favorites are stored encrypted at Cloudflare. We do not sell or share anything. You can delete your account anytime.
faq.a3: Yes. It is a progressive web app (PWA) — you install it from the browser and it behaves like a native app. Works on iOS, Android, any tablet or laptop.
faq.q4: Where do the translations come from?
faq.a4: Romanian version: Biblia Cornilescu (VDC). Spanish version: Reina Valera (RVL). These are public-domain translations or used with permission.
faq.a5: Yes — corrections, new translations, features. The code is on GitHub. And prayers count.

final.title: Let's read.
final.text: No account. No app to download. Just Scripture, in your language, on any screen.
